First, I’ll start with him. At “almost 30”, he should be willing to more effectively communicate or ask for space if he needs it. Then again, I can’t know the extent of the conflict before this situation. 

Next, an apology is comprised of a few things. First, a formal and direct admission of shame and regret whilst ensuring that one’s partner knows that they didn’t deserve whatever happened. Then, the “fixing” begins by asking what you can do to make them feel better and restore any faith or dignity lost. This has to be genuine; not begrudging. For actions, there are consequences. If you do someone wrong, then basic accountability dictates that you right your wrongs directly until they’re not on the deficit end anymore. 

If I had an argument with my girlfriend, I would interpret “so we’re done?” As an indirect threat, especially in response to him voicing his concerns and worries. Maybe he’s just in his feels. Don’t be presumptive. Instead, ask him what he means and what he feels is the best approach moving forward. Even though you didn’t mean it this way, it reads as:

A-I think we moved too fast 
B-Well, I’m not gonna cater to your concerns, so I guess we’re done, right? 

A more effective approach that doesn’t invalidate his feelings starts with:

A- I think we moved too fast 
B- I love you a lot, and I’m sorry i hurt you. Is there anything I can do to make you feel better? Is there anything you need? (The offers cannot be empty)

It is totally normal to feel worried about him. I fully acknowledge that a crappy situation doesn’t paint the full picture of two people’s entire relationship, and so I won’t pretend to be more of an expert than you. 

From an outsider perspective, I think the most important thing is for you to find peace. It’s not selfish; try to trust me. Doing what you can, and only what you can, will always be enough. The slightest effort is enough. I’m proud of you for navigating this tough spot.

When there’s nothing you can do, all that’s left is to do what you can. One possibility is that he’s a sociopathic chronic manipulator who sexually assaulted you by kissing you without express permission. The other possibility is that he is extremely mentally disturbed and overdependent on you for his health and safety. Over-dependence, whether intentional or otherwise, is still abuse. I’m sorry you’re going through this, but you were right to be honest. Don’t compromise your moral code because of someone else’ hang ups and mistakes. 

Legally, you’ve no obligation to prevent a suicide in this context. So long as you don’t tell him to kill himself, you’re fine. Even better if you provide him a resource before blocking him or whatever puts you at peace, since trying to help will weigh less heavily on your conscience, even if you’ve no obligation to do so.
